questions.question: A 22-year-old man is evaluated for 3 months of persecutory delusions that his coworkers are transmitting his thoughts to a podcast, along with disorganized speech and declining work performance. His mother reports he was entirely well until this spring. He has never had a manic or depressive episode, drinks alcohol rarely, and urine toxicology and a comprehensive metabolic panel are unremarkable. MRI of the brain is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis at this point in his course?

explanations.A: Brief psychotic disorder requires resolution within 1 month, and his symptoms have already persisted for 3 months without remission.
explanations.B: Delusional disorder excludes prominent disorganized speech and requires relatively preserved functioning apart from the delusional theme.
explanations.C: Full criterion A symptoms present for more than 1 month but less than 6 months, without a mood episode or substance cause, define schizophreniform disorder; the diagnosis converts to schizophrenia if illness persists beyond 6 months.
explanations.D: Schizotypal personality disorder involves lifelong odd beliefs and eccentric behavior without frank delusions or an acute decline from a prior level of function.
explanations.E: A substance-induced psychotic disorder requires temporal linkage to intoxication or withdrawal, and his toxicology screen is negative with only rare alcohol use.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman with a decade of progressive cognitive decline, psychosis, and choreiform movements has a normal brain MRI and EEG. The team plans genetic testing for Huntington disease. Her 24-year-old asymptomatic daughter asks what the diagnosis would mean for her. Which of the following statements is most accurate to provide during pretest counseling?

answers.A: Disease onset occurs at essentially the same age in every affected member of a family
answers.B: Her risk of inheriting the expanded CAG allele is 50%, and onset may occur earlier in successive generations
answers.C: Symptoms will develop only if she inherits an expanded allele from both parents
answers.D: Testing should be deferred until she develops involuntary movements or cognitive symptoms
answers.E: The disorder arises from a mitochondrial mutation and is therefore transmitted only through the maternal line

explanations.A: Age of onset varies within families because of anticipation, which reflects further expansion of the CAG repeat during transmission.
explanations.B: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the expanded HTT CAG repeat, and repeat instability produces anticipation with earlier onset in later generations.
explanations.C: Huntington disease is dominantly inherited; a single expanded allele is sufficient to cause disease.
explanations.D: Predictive testing is available to asymptomatic at-risk adults with appropriate counseling, and waiting for motor signs offers no benefit for reproductive or life planning.
explanations.E: The causative mutation is a nuclear trinucleotide repeat expansion in HTT on chromosome 4, not a mitochondrial mutation.

questions.question: A 24-year-old graduate student is brought to the emergency department by his roommates after 9 days of sleeping only 2 hours per night, talking so rapidly that others cannot interrupt him, spending $14,000 on recording equipment, and announcing that he has been chosen as a prophet who can heal illness by touch. He has had two prior episodes of depression but has never had psychotic symptoms between episodes. Urine toxicology is negative, TSH is normal, and head CT is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.A: Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic, with psychotic features
answers.B: Delirium due to another medical condition

explanations.A: Grandiose delusions arising only within a manic episode of decreased sleep need, pressured speech, and reckless spending indicate bipolar I disorder with psychotic features.
explanations.B: Delirium is marked by a fluctuating level of consciousness and impaired attention with an identifiable medical cause, none of which is present here.
explanations.C: Schizoaffective disorder requires psychosis for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a mood episode, and he is asymptomatic between episodes.
explanations.D: Schizophrenia would require psychotic symptoms independent of mood episodes and typically prominent negative symptoms with functional decline between episodes.
explanations.E: A stimulant-induced psychosis would follow documented stimulant use and is not supported by a negative urine toxicology screen.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man admitted with a first episode of psychosis is started on aripiprazole, and his persecutory delusions improve substantially over 2 weeks. He then reports an unbearable inner restlessness and is observed pacing the hallway continuously, shifting his feet while seated, and stating he would rather stop the drug than "feel like this." There is no rigidity, tremor, fever, or abnormal involuntary tongue or facial movement, and his creatine kinase is normal. Which of the following adverse effects is he most likely experiencing?

explanations.A: Acute dystonia causes sustained involuntary muscle contractions such as torticollis or oculogyric crisis, typically within hours to days of starting therapy.
explanations.B: A subjective sense of inner restlessness with an irresistible urge to move is akathisia, a common and highly distressing adverse effect of aripiprazole that frequently drives nonadherence.
explanations.C: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome presents with fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, and markedly elevated creatine kinase, all of which are absent.
explanations.D: Drug-induced parkinsonism produces bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, and tremor rather than restlessness with normal tone.
explanations.E: Tardive dyskinesia consists of involuntary choreoathetoid orofacial movements emerging after months to years of exposure, not 2 weeks.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman is admitted after 3 weeks of rapidly progressive behavioral change beginning with insomnia and paranoid delusions and progressing to disorganized speech, agitation, and two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. On examination she has intermittent orofacial dyskinesias, labile blood pressure, and tachycardia alternating with bradycardia. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 5-cm complex right ovarian mass. Cerebrospinal fluid studies are shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.E: Systemic lupus erythematosus with CNS involvement

explanations.A: Subacute psychosis in a young woman followed by seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, and autonomic instability with a lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis and an ovarian teratoma is the classic presentation of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
explanations.B: Herpes simplex encephalitis causes fever with temporal lobe hemorrhagic changes and a positive CSF HSV PCR, which is negative here.
explanations.C: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows dopamine antagonist exposure and produces lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, and elevated creatine kinase, not a CSF pleocytosis or teratoma.
explanations.D: Schizophrenia does not cause seizures, autonomic instability, or an inflammatory CSF profile, and its onset is not this abrupt.
explanations.E: Neuropsychiatric lupus would be accompanied by systemic features such as rash, arthritis, cytopenias, or nephritis and would not be explained by an ovarian teratoma.

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman has had persecutory delusions and derogatory auditory hallucinations nearly continuously for 3 years. During that time she has also had two 3-month major depressive episodes with anhedonia, hypersomnia, and suicidal ideation. Her psychiatrist documents that after each depressive episode resolved, the voices and paranoia persisted unchanged for 3 to 4 months while her mood was euthymic. She uses no substances, and urine toxicology is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.A: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features
answers.B: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

explanations.A: Bipolar I disorder requires a manic episode, and she has had only depressive episodes.
explanations.B: In major depressive disorder with psychotic features, psychosis occurs exclusively during the mood episode; her psychosis persists for months while she is euthymic.
explanations.C: Psychosis lasting 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode, combined with mood episodes that occupy the majority of the illness, defines schizoaffective disorder, depressive type.
explanations.D: Schizophrenia can include brief mood symptoms, but here full depressive episodes account for the majority of the total illness duration, which mandates the schizoaffective diagnosis.
explanations.E: A substance-induced psychotic disorder requires a temporally linked substance exposure, which is absent with negative toxicology and no reported use.

questions.question: A 63-year-old man with no psychiatric history is admitted after 2 weeks of paranoid behavior and visual misperceptions. On mental status examination he has waxing and waning alertness, is unkempt and uncooperative, has slurred speech and psychomotor retardation, and alternates between somnolence and agitation. He voices persecutory ideation that his wife is having an affair, his thought process is tangential, and his insight and judgment are impaired. He scores 16/30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination, missing points on orientation and attention. Which of the following findings is the strongest indicator that his psychosis is due to delirium rather than a primary psychotic disorder?

answers.B: Paranoid ideation regarding his wife's fidelity
answers.E: Waxing and waning alertness with impaired attention

explanations.A: Impaired insight and judgment are nearly universal in active psychosis of any cause and do not discriminate between delirium and schizophrenia.
explanations.B: Delusions of infidelity occur in delirium, delusional disorder, and schizophrenia alike, so their content is not diagnostic.
explanations.C: Slurred speech and psychomotor slowing suggest sedation or intoxication but can also be seen with antipsychotic effects and are not the defining feature of delirium.
explanations.D: Tangentiality is a form of thought disorder common to many psychotic presentations and is not specific to a medical etiology.
explanations.E: An acutely fluctuating level of consciousness with a primary deficit in attention is the cardinal feature of delirium; attention and level of arousal are characteristically preserved in primary psychotic disorders.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man is newly diagnosed with schizophrenia. His mother also has schizophrenia and is chronically homeless. His 23-year-old sister, who has no psychiatric symptoms, asks the treating physician how likely she is to develop the same illness. Which of the following best describes her lifetime risk?

answers.A: Approximately 1%, the same as the general population
answers.B: Approximately 10%, roughly tenfold the general population risk
answers.C: Approximately 25%, as expected for autosomal recessive inheritance
answers.D: Approximately 50%, as expected for autosomal dominant inheritance

explanations.A: Roughly 1% is the baseline population risk, but having affected first-degree relatives raises her risk well above baseline.
explanations.B: A first-degree relative of someone with schizophrenia carries a lifetime risk on the order of 10%, about ten times the general population risk, reflecting polygenic liability rather than Mendelian transmission.
explanations.C: Schizophrenia is polygenic and multifactorial; it does not follow autosomal recessive inheritance, and a 25% figure has no basis.
explanations.D: A 50% risk would imply single-gene autosomal dominant inheritance, which is inconsistent with the known genetic architecture of schizophrenia.
explanations.E: Monozygotic twin concordance is approximately 40-50%, not 90%, and in any case does not apply to a non-twin sibling.

questions.question: A 34-year-old veteran presents for evaluation of chronic mood instability that worsened after a 12-month deployment. For 5 years he has used cocaine, initially to stay awake and avoid combat nightmares. He reports that cocaine now makes him irritable and paranoid but he cannot stop. Last weekend, within an hour of using cocaine, he became convinced that police were coming to arrest him, hid his supply, and armed himself when he heard a knock at the door. By the next day he recognized that no one had been coming for him and felt horrified by what nearly happened. Between periods of use he has no delusions, hallucinations, or negative symptoms. Which of the following features best supports a cocaine-induced psychotic disorder rather than a primary psychotic disorder?

answers.A: Onset of paranoia only in the hours after cocaine use, with insight restored afterward
answers.B: Paranoid rather than grandiose content of his delusional beliefs
answers.C: Persistence of vivid combat nightmares for a decade after his deployment
answers.D: Presence of a major psychosocial stressor preceding his first symptoms
answers.E: Symptom onset in his late twenties rather than during late adolescence

explanations.A: Psychotic symptoms that appear only in close temporal relationship to intoxication and remit with restored insight between exposures are the defining feature of a substance-induced psychotic disorder.
explanations.B: Persecutory content is the most common delusional theme in both primary psychotic disorders and stimulant-induced psychosis, so it has no discriminating value.
explanations.C: Recurrent trauma-related nightmares support comorbid post-traumatic stress disorder but say nothing about the etiology of the paranoia.
explanations.D: Psychosocial stressors can precipitate exacerbations of primary psychotic disorders as well, so a stressor does not establish a substance etiology.
explanations.E: Onset in the late twenties is entirely compatible with a primary psychotic disorder, particularly in men presenting slightly later than the typical peak.

questions.question: A 20-year-old male university student is brought to the emergency department after walking into a former professor's classroom and shouting, "I am with the FBI and I am here to tell you all the truth." Over the preceding 14 months he stopped seeing friends, spent most days lying in bed staring at the ceiling, rarely spoke to his roommates, and was suspended for not attending class; his sister has frequently seen him mumbling quietly to himself. In the emergency department he refuses hospital food because he believes it is poisoned and tells the physician she lacks sufficient clearance to discuss his FBI work. He appears internally preoccupied but denies hallucinations, and he denies any current or prior manic or depressive episodes. Urine toxicology is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Brief psychotic disorder requires symptoms lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month with full return to baseline, whereas this patient has been declining continuously for more than a year.
explanations.B: Delusional disorder requires delusions without prominent negative symptoms, disorganization, or functional deterioration, but this patient has marked avolition, social withdrawal, and academic failure.
explanations.C: Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with active psychosis for the majority of the illness, and he explicitly denies any manic or depressive episodes.
explanations.D: Continuous signs of illness for more than 6 months with persecutory delusions, apparent internal preoccupation, and prominent negative symptoms (avolition, asociality, alogia) causing functional decline meets criteria for schizophrenia.
explanations.E: Schizophreniform disorder is reserved for episodes lasting 1 to 6 months; his prodromal and active symptoms span roughly 14 months, which crosses the 6-month threshold into schizophrenia.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man is brought in by his daughter for 1 year of recurrent, detailed visual hallucinations of small children playing in the living room. His alertness and attention fluctuate markedly from hour to hour, and his wife reports that for several years he has shouted and punched during sleep as though acting out dreams. Over the past 6 months he has developed bradykinesia and mild rigidity. He was given a single dose of haloperidol in the emergency department last month and became profoundly rigid and unresponsive for 2 days. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Alzheimer disease begins with insidious episodic memory loss, and prominent early visual hallucinations with fluctuating cognition and parkinsonism are atypical.
explanations.B: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, parkinsonism developing after cognitive symptoms, and severe neuroleptic sensitivity are the core features of dementia with Lewy bodies.
explanations.C: Huntington disease produces chorea with midlife onset and an autosomal dominant family history, not visual hallucinations with parkinsonism in the eighth decade.
explanations.D: In Parkinson disease dementia the motor syndrome precedes cognitive and psychotic symptoms by at least a year, whereas here hallucinations and cognitive fluctuation came first.
explanations.E: Very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis features persecutory delusions with preserved cognition and does not cause parkinsonism or neuroleptic hypersensitivity.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with schizophrenia diagnosed at age 19 has taken olanzapine for the past year with good control of her persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. She has been fully adherent and wants to find a job and live independently, but she has gained 16 kg since starting the drug. Her waist circumference is 106 cm and blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. Fasting laboratory results are shown. Which of the following antipsychotics is the most appropriate substitution?

explanations.A: Aripiprazole carries the lowest risk of weight gain, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia among commonly used antipsychotics, making it the best choice for a patient who has developed metabolic syndrome on olanzapine.
explanations.B: Chlorpromazine is a low-potency first-generation agent associated with sedation, orthostasis, and weight gain, offering no metabolic advantage.
explanations.C: Clozapine has the highest metabolic burden of any antipsychotic and is reserved for treatment-resistant illness, not for a patient responding well to therapy.
explanations.D: Paliperidone carries intermediate metabolic risk along with the highest rates of hyperprolactinemia, so it does not address her problem.
explanations.E: Quetiapine has metabolic liability comparable to olanzapine and would be expected to perpetuate her weight gain and dyslipidemia.

questions.question: A 63-year-old businessman with coronary artery disease and chronic back pain is found down on the road and brought in by EMS; psychiatry is consulted for "psychotic behavior." His family reports 2 weeks of running around with knives, sending paranoid e-mails, seeing people in the walls, accusing his wife of an affair, and not sleeping. He has no psychiatric history. His outpatient medications are metoprolol, MS-Contin, hydroxyzine as needed for sleep, and diphenhydramine as needed for allergies; a box containing numerous medication bottles was found in his car. Examination and studies are shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his altered mental status?

answers.A: Anticholinergic delirium from diphenhydramine and hydroxyzine
answers.C: Opioid withdrawal from abrupt discontinuation of morphine

explanations.A: Mydriasis, hypoactive bowel sounds, and urinary retention in a sedated, delirious older adult taking two potent anticholinergic agents (plus an opioid) point to anticholinergic delirium; standard urine toxicology screens do not detect these drugs.
explanations.B: Beta-blocker toxicity causes bradycardia and hypotension rather than mydriasis, urinary retention, and ileus, and his ECG and vital signs were unremarkable.
explanations.C: Opioid withdrawal produces mydriasis but with hyperactive bowel sounds, diarrhea, lacrimation, piloerection, and agitation rather than sedation with ileus and retention.
explanations.D: Serotonin syndrome requires a serotonergic agent and causes hyperreflexia, clonus, hyperthermia, and diaphoresis, the opposite of his depressed reflexes.
explanations.E: Wernicke encephalopathy presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion in a thiamine-deficient patient, and there is no history of alcohol use or malnutrition here.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman is admitted after 3 months of progressively worsening depressed mood, 12-kg weight loss, early morning awakening, and psychomotor retardation. She now states with complete conviction that her intestines have rotted away and that she is being punished for a minor tax error she made decades ago; she refuses food for this reason. She has had no psychotic symptoms at any time when her mood was normal, and her one prior episode 12 years ago remitted fully with treatment. Urine toxicology and brain MRI are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.B: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

explanations.A: Delusional disorder requires the absence of a prominent mood episode driving the presentation; here a full melancholic depressive episode is the primary disturbance.
explanations.B: Mood-congruent nihilistic and guilt delusions occurring exclusively during a major depressive episode, with no psychosis during euthymia, define major depressive disorder with psychotic features.
explanations.C: Schizoaffective disorder requires at least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations in the absence of a major mood episode, which she has never had.
explanations.D: Schizophrenia would require psychotic symptoms that persist independently of mood episodes plus 6 months of continuous illness with negative symptoms.
explanations.E: Schizophreniform disorder is diagnosed only when a mood disorder with psychotic features has been excluded, and her psychosis is entirely confined to the depressive episode.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with schizophrenia is brought to the emergency department by police after she tried to force a bus driver out of his seat, believing he was kidnapping her. She has had multiple hospitalizations since her first episode at age 19, each preceded by her stopping medication. Her psychiatrist notes that at a visit 3 months ago she reported no hallucinations and seemed less paranoid, but the team now learns she stopped taking olanzapine 2 months ago. She is restabilized on the same agent within 10 days and endorses a goal of living independently. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce her risk of relapse?

answers.B: Increase the oral olanzapine dose above the usual maximum
answers.E: Switch to a low-potency first-generation antipsychotic

explanations.A: Lithium augmentation does not address nonadherence and has limited evidence in non-affective psychosis.
explanations.B: Escalating the oral dose cannot help a patient who is not taking the medication and only increases metabolic and sedative burden.
explanations.C: Because medication nonadherence is the leading cause of relapse in schizophrenia, a long-acting injectable guarantees delivery and makes lapses immediately visible to the treatment team.
explanations.D: Clozapine is indicated for treatment resistance, not for relapse due to nonadherence, and its weekly blood monitoring would be difficult for a nonadherent patient.
explanations.E: First-generation low-potency agents add anticholinergic and extrapyramidal burden without improving adherence.

questions.question: A 48-year-old accountant is brought to clinic by his wife because for 2 years he has been convinced that his next-door neighbor is poisoning his lawn and intercepting his mail; he has filed multiple police reports and installed cameras facing the property line. He continues to work full time with excellent performance reviews, maintains his hygiene, and enjoys his usual hobbies. He denies hallucinations, his speech is logical and goal-directed, and there is no evidence of avolition or flat affect. Urine toxicology and laboratory studies are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: A non-bizarre delusion of at least 1 month's duration with otherwise preserved functioning and no other criterion A symptoms is characteristic of delusional disorder, persecutory type.
explanations.B: Paranoid personality disorder involves pervasive suspiciousness and mistrust but stops short of a fixed, encapsulated delusional belief held with absolute conviction.
explanations.C: Schizoaffective disorder requires prominent mood episodes alongside psychosis, and no depressive or manic episode is described.
explanations.D: Schizophrenia requires two or more criterion A symptoms with functional decline; he has an isolated delusion with entirely intact work and social functioning.
explanations.E: Schizotypal personality disorder is a lifelong pattern of odd beliefs, magical thinking, and interpersonal deficits rather than a single sustained persecutory delusion.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman is brought in by her sister 10 days after her husband was killed in a motor vehicle collision. For the past 8 days she has insisted that her husband's employer faked his death and is monitoring her apartment through the smoke detectors, and her speech frequently derails mid-sentence. She had no prior psychiatric history and was working full time until the accident. Urine toxicology is negative, and she is started on a low-dose antipsychotic. Three weeks later she has returned entirely to her premorbid level of functioning with no residual symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.B: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

explanations.A: Delusions and disorganized speech lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month, often following a marked stressor, with complete return to premorbid functioning defines brief psychotic disorder.
explanations.B: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features requires a full 2-week depressive episode with the psychosis occurring exclusively during that episode, which was not described here.
explanations.C: Post-traumatic stress disorder involves reexperiencing, avoidance, negative cognitions, and hyperarousal rather than fixed persecutory delusions and formal thought disorder.
explanations.D: Schizophrenia requires 6 months of continuous illness, which is incompatible with complete resolution within a few weeks.
explanations.E: Schizophreniform disorder requires symptoms to persist longer than 1 month; her episode remitted well before that threshold.

questions.question: A 34-year-old veteran of a 12-month combat deployment is evaluated for symptoms that began after his return and have worsened over a decade. He describes feeling "on automatic pilot" and no longer enjoying his wife or children, scans crowded public places constantly for threats, avoids driving over bridges, and has nightmares of "bombs and land mines" several nights a week. He occasionally hears a squadmate who died overseas call his name while he is reliving the event, but he knows the voice is not real and never hears it otherwise. He denies delusions and has no negative symptoms or functional decline outside of these episodes. Which of the following best explains his symptoms?

explanations.A: A substance-induced psychotic disorder would require symptoms temporally tied to intoxication or withdrawal, not trauma-specific reexperiencing with preserved reality testing.
explanations.B: Generalized anxiety disorder involves excessive worry across many life domains rather than trauma-specific intrusions, avoidance, and hypervigilance.
explanations.C: Reexperiencing (nightmares, trauma-linked pseudohallucinations with intact insight), avoidance of reminders, negative alterations in mood, and hyperarousal after a life-threatening event define post-traumatic stress disorder.
explanations.D: Schizophrenia requires true hallucinations or delusions with lost insight plus 6 months of illness including negative symptoms and functional decline, none of which he has.
explanations.E: Schizotypal personality disorder is a lifelong pattern of odd beliefs and social deficits, not a syndrome beginning after a discrete traumatic exposure.

questions.question: A 54-year-old former waitress is brought by her husband for evaluation. She was "completely fine" until her early forties, when she quit work because of dropped trays, misremembered orders, and irritability. Over the ensuing decade she has seen multiple psychiatrists and been prescribed antidepressants, antipsychotics, anxiolytics, and mood stabilizers without benefit. She now has daily visual hallucinations of a judge she throws bombs at and persecutory delusions. Examination shows psychomotor slowing, blunted affect, and involuntary "dancelike" movements of the trunk and arms; she is fully oriented with intact attention but has marked short- and long-term memory impairment. Her mother died at 70 after years of severe dementia, postural instability, and involuntary movements, and her maternal grandfather became ill in his late fifties and died by suicide at 62. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.D: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

explanations.A: Dementia with Lewy bodies produces fluctuating attention, well-formed visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism, not choreiform movements with a clear autosomal dominant family history.
explanations.B: Midlife onset of psychiatric symptoms and cognitive decline with chorea, plus an autosomal dominant family history including a demented parent and a grandfather who died by suicide, is classic for Huntington disease.
explanations.C: Late-onset schizophrenia does not produce progressive amnesia, chorea, or a family history of a movement disorder with dementia.
explanations.D: Depression with psychotic features would show mood-congruent delusions confined to a discrete episode and would not explain the chorea or a decade of progressive cognitive decline.
explanations.E: Wilson disease typically presents before age 40 with Kayser-Fleischer rings, tremor or dystonia, and hepatic dysfunction rather than midlife chorea with dominant inheritance.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with no psychiatric history is evaluated for 2 months of persecutory delusions that her coworkers are recording her, accompanied by auditory hallucinations. Her husband adds that over the same period she has been profoundly fatigued, cold all the time, and constipated, and has gained 8 kg. On examination her skin is dry, her voice is hoarse, and deep tendon reflexes show delayed relaxation. Urine toxicology is negative and head CT is normal. Laboratory results are shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her psychosis?

explanations.A: Severe hypothyroidism with a markedly elevated TSH, low free T4, hyponatremia, and elevated creatine kinase can produce psychosis ("myxedema madness"), which typically resolves with thyroid hormone replacement.
explanations.B: Neurosyphilis can cause psychosis and personality change but would present with Argyll Robertson pupils, tabetic findings, or reactive treponemal serologies rather than a myxedematous picture.
explanations.C: Schizophrenia is a diagnosis of exclusion and cannot be made when a reversible medical cause fully accounts for the psychosis, as the thyroid studies do here.
explanations.D: Neuropsychiatric lupus would be accompanied by rash, arthritis, serositis, cytopenias, or renal involvement, none of which is described.
explanations.E: Her vitamin B12 level is normal, so deficiency-related neuropsychiatric disease is excluded.
